# Part A — MapReduce and Hadoop {#sec-s14-a}

**You cannot move 10 Terabytes of data to the calculator. You must move the calculator to the data.**

## 1. Big Data Analytics using Map Reduce {#sec-s14-topic-1}

**MapReduce is a programming paradigm that splits a massive calculation into two distinct phases: Map (filtering/sorting across many machines) and Reduce (aggregating the final results).**

It exists because traditional databases try to drag all the data into the central processor to sum it up. Over a network, moving 10 Terabytes of data takes hours. MapReduce solves this by sending a tiny 1-kilobyte script to the 100 computers where the data *already lives*, having them do the math locally, and only sending the tiny final answer back over the network.

::: {.callout-tip title="🧠 Analogy — The Ballot Counters"}
**The everyday thing:** Counting 10 million votes in a national election.

**The mapping:** 
- **Traditional:** You bring all 10 million paper ballots to one guy in the capital city. He counts them one by one. It takes a year.
- **Map Phase:** Every individual polling station (the distributed computers) counts their own 10,000 ballots locally.
- **Reduce Phase:** Each station phones in their final tally (just two numbers: Candidate A: 6000, Candidate B: 4000) to the capital. The capital just adds those small numbers together. The election is decided in an hour.
:::

### How it works

- **Map:** Extracts the relevant data. (e.g., "Look at this server's logs, and count every time you see 'Error 404'").
- **Shuffle:** Groups similar data together.
- **Reduce:** Sums it all up. (e.g., "Add up all the 404 counts from all 100 servers into one grand total").

### ❓ MCQs

**Q1.** What is the primary bottleneck that MapReduce avoids by processing data locally where it sits on the hard drive?

- (a) CPU processing speed.
- (b) **Network transfer speed (Moving massive data across wires is slow).**
- (c) Monitor refresh rates.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answers"}
**A1 — (b).** It is always faster to send a small Python script to a server than it is to send 500GB of data from that server to your laptop.
:::

# Part B — Apache Spark {#sec-s14-b}

**Hadoop wrote everything to disk. Spark keeps it all in RAM.**

## 2. Apache Hadoop vs Apache Spark {#sec-s14-topic-2}

**Apache Spark is the modern, lightning-fast successor to Hadoop's MapReduce engine.**

It exists because Hadoop was slow. Between the Map phase and the Reduce phase, Hadoop wrote all intermediate results to physical hard drives to prevent data loss if a server crashed. Reading and writing from physical hard drives is slow. Spark, instead, keeps all intermediate data purely in RAM (memory).

### How it works

Spark operates using **RDDs (Resilient Distributed Datasets)** or **DataFrames**. If a server crashes while holding data in RAM, Spark just looks at the history of how that data was made (the "lineage") and instantly recalculates it on another server.

Because RAM is 100x faster than hard drives, Spark runs 100x faster than Hadoop for many machine learning tasks.

# Part Demo — PySpark vs Pandas {#sec-s14-demo}

**Running a PySpark DataFrame script.**

Pandas syntax and PySpark syntax look similar, but under the hood, Spark is orchestrating 100 machines.

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Note: You need a Spark Cluster to run this.
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, count

# 1. Initialize the Spark Cluster connection
spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("LogAnalyzer").getOrCreate()

# 2. Read a massive 500GB distributed file
# Spark doesn't actually read it yet! It uses "Lazy Evaluation". It just remembers the command.
df_logs = spark.read.csv("hdfs://user/logs/massive_logs.csv", header=True)

# 3. Perform a Map and Reduce operation
# We filter for errors, group by the server IP, and count them.
error_counts = (df_logs
    .filter(col("status_code") == 404)     # Map Phase
    .groupBy("server_ip")                  # Shuffle Phase
    .agg(count("*").alias("error_count"))  # Reduce Phase
)

# 4. Trigger the computation!
# Up until this point, Spark did zero math. The .show() command forces it to execute 
# the massive distributed plan and fetch the top 5 results.
error_counts.orderBy(col("error_count").desc()).show(5)
```

::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ The trap of Lazy Evaluation"}
In Pandas, when you write `df.filter()`, it happens instantly. In Spark, it does *nothing* until you call an "Action" like `.show()` or `.collect()`. If you write a 50-line script and make a typo on line 2, Spark won't tell you there's an error until line 51 when you finally ask to see the result!
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="✅ Before you move on"}
- [ ] Understand why Spark is drastically faster than traditional Hadoop MapReduce.
- [ ] **The one thing from this chapter that is easiest to forget:** Spark uses Lazy Evaluation. It builds an execution plan and waits for an action before crunching the numbers.
:::
